fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Tolkien's Catholicism Was Not a Label", "body": "Chance opens by asking whether Tolkien's faith might be Catholic only in the sense of universal, older and wider than the church. Rachel Fulton Brown pushes back hard. He was Roman Catholic and he meant it. She walks through the cost: his mother Mabel converting from Anglicanism and being abandoned by her family, dying and leaving Ronald and Hilary orphaned under Father Frank Morgan, and Tolkien obeying that guardian for years before writing to Edith at midnight and telling her she had to become Catholic first. Conviction, she argues, is measured by what a person sacrificed for it."}, {"title": "Mythopoeia and the Argument With Lewis", "body": "The centerpiece of the first half is Tolkien's poem Mythopoeia, published in Tree and Leaf alongside On Fairy Stories and Leaf by Niggle. Rachel reads a long passage aloud, including the lines about man as sub-creator, the refracted light splintered from a single white, and the closing claim that we make still by the law in which we're made. She explains that Tolkien wrote it in the early 1930s to answer C.S. Lewis, who held that myths were lies breathed through silver. Tolkien answered in verse rather than argument, and Lewis eventually became a Christian."}, {"title": "Why Creation Happens Through Music", "body": "Rachel connects the Ainulindale to the medieval quadrivium and the discarded image of the cosmos. Arithmetic is number, geometry is space, music is time, and astronomy puts them together. Both Tolkien and Lewis worked inside the old Ptolemaic picture of rotating spheres whose movement makes music we can no longer hear. She points to Michael Ward's book Planet Narnia, which reads each Narnia volume as governed by a planet, and to the Space Trilogy, where Earth is the silent planet. Eru proposes a pattern, and the pattern he proposes is inevitably a song."}, {"title": "Melkor, Dissonance, and Misused Free Will", "body": "Chance frames Melkor as a fallen demiurge who seeks the secret of the eternal fire and imposes his own theme on the music. Rachel reframes it as Tolkien's meditation on why anyone turns away from harmony at all. In her Tolkien class at the University of Chicago she plays Beethoven, plainchant, Hildegard, Smetana and a Blind Guardian track to make students hear the difference. Her key point is that Melkor's theme resembles the sorrowful third theme, which is exactly why humanity finds it attractive. Tolkien wanted the effects of sin and misused free will made visible and physical."}, {"title": "Makers Devoured by What They Make", "body": "The conversation turns to possession. Feanor makes the Silmarils, gems holding the blended light of the Two Trees, and falls because he will not let them be broken to save the Trees, which leads to the first kinslaying. Rachel calls the general problem idolatry, the thing we grow so attached to that we cannot let go, the precious. She extends it to writing itself as an early Enochian gift from fallen angels, and to artificial intelligence, which she says is made entirely out of writing. Chance adds that Mordor reads as an allegory for industrialization."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Professor Rachel Fulton Brown joins InnerVerse to talk Tolkien! In this lively discussion we explore Tolkien's mytho-mystic Christian convictions as allegorized in his great works, the Lord of the Rings and its massive legendarium. Topics include the Logos, Eros, the Gods & planets, and the purpose of evil and dissonance. What does it mean to be a creator in a created world?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we examine world mountain and axis mundi symbolism, Earendil and Anglo Saxon literature, strategic philology, the unfinished sequel to the LOTR story, why civilizations fall, and the mystery of cryptid creatures and alternate humanoids of folklore.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A Mythology Recovered From Christian Poems", "body": "Rachel Fulton Brown explains that Tolkien felt compelled to write because England has almost no stories from its Anglo-Saxon past before conversion, and nearly all surviving Old English poetry was set down by Christians, with Beowulf the rare exception that still passed through a Christian pen. She traces the name Earendel to a series of Advent lyrics called The Christ, where the line hails Earendel as the brightest of angels sent over Middle-earth to men, and describes Tolkien asking what world could have held that name. Chance Garton links the world axis to Polaris, the fixed point with a dragon turning around it."}, {"title": "Two Ways of Reading Words", "body": "The conversation turns into a friendly standoff over method. Chance plays association games across languages, linking Earendil and Ireland to Etruscan roots, Britain to the Hebrew word for covenant, and tin to the Etruscan sky father Tinia. Rachel answers that philology was a nineteenth century science of sound changes, requiring a real grounding in phonemes, syntax and grammar, and recalls Tolkien scolding a reader who guessed that Sauron must mean dinosaur. She recommends The Notion Club Papers, calls Chance a poet, and agrees that poetry and measured speech are one way the divine reaches us, which is why her Draco Alchemicus project is written in Spenserian stanzas."}, {"title": "The New Shadow and the Falling of Nations", "body": "Chance reads Tolkien's letter about an abandoned sequel set a century after the downfall of Sauron, in which the people of Gondor grow restless with peace, a secret Satanistic cult takes root and boys play at being Orcs. Rachel suggests Tolkien had already told the Fall many times, through Melkor, Feanor and Numenor, and that an artist can pour everything into one great work and lack the energy to make another. She notes he lived through two world wars and knew evil keeps reconstituting itself. Chance frames destruction as regeneration, like winter, while Rachel describes death as the gift of Iluvatar and the Numenoreans' clutching at life as their undoing."}, {"title": "The Maker Inside His Own Story", "body": "Rachel argues that the doctrine of the Trinity is less a puzzle about threeness than an attempt to explain how the creator of everything could enter his own story as a character, a question Tolkien stages in the dialogue between Finrod and Andreth. Chance says he is less concerned with a historical savior than with the pattern behind the story, and Rachel agrees that people constantly turn their artifacts into idols, from the Bible to arguments over the Filioque. She closes the thread with Tolkien's Letter 310, where the purpose of life is to praise the creator, and Chance ties that praise to authentic gratitude."}, {"title": "Cryptids, Elves and the Edges of Consciousness", "body": "Asked about cryptids, Rachel says she believes in angels and demons and sees many strange encounters as meetings with fallen intelligences. She reads Aule's dwarves as a lesson in letting go, since Aule's willingness to destroy them is what lets Iluvatar give them life, and points to Ronald Hutton as the best guide to British folklore, barrow tombs and the green man. Chance connects dwarves to real underground tunnel networks, compares fairy contact with alien abduction lore, and proposes that demons may be clinging human dead. Rachel counters that sudden aliens are historically nonsensical, and shares a colleague's view that the elves of medieval stories are the dead."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "Almost everything we know of pagan Germanic mythology is translated through Christian themes and tropes already.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Philology is not simply finding things that sound the same in words and then thinking that they fit together.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You have to be able to go the left brain and right brain route. Look at things prosaically and poetically.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We feel as modern people have lost the mythology as much because we've lost the literal poetry.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I think one big purpose of life is life itself. The continuing of life is its own end and its own meaning.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Tolkien, he's very aware of the problem of trying to control everything by never letting it change, which is what you're trying to do when you're trying not to die.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "People can make the Bible as artifact into an idol. It happens all the time.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I think life is way more enjoyable when you're praising the creator, when you have gratitude, authentic gratitude.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I don't believe in aliens either, but I also don't think we're on a ball flying through an infinite void of nothingness with zero meaning.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It's not that suddenly aliens discovered the United States in 1950 and started visiting us. That, as a historian, I find completely nonsensical.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/41bef718-7a0c-434a-9a9b-7201b0c88652/RACHEL-FULTON-BROWN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "people come to Tolkien wanting to be inside that story and one of the things I do in the course is sort of say, well, what he thought he was doing was showing you the way in which, as he says in Mythopoeia, we make still by the law in which we're made", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "And the question is like, are those keys there because we're looking at a system, a craft that had a common origin and then spread out or are those keys there of consistency because we're talking about true events?", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "And understanding that this desire to see the single truth in all of these mythologies, I'm sorry, but it is a Christian desire.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "the main character goes out, outside of the influence of the Earth and out of the silent planet. Earth is silent because we can't hear the music of the spheres anymore.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "And so with Melkor's ability to know somewhat of what the other gods are gonna do, he then starts to try to impose his own creation outside of the intended music, thus birthing dissonance or evil into the world.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The obverse of we are made still by the law, we make still by the law in which we're made, is that we can become so attached to the things that we've made that they destroy us.", "author": "Rachel Fulton Brown", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "So never be afraid of the end of one story and the beginning of another, because that's really, in my opinion, all the transition probably is. You exist, you will always exist.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "To be able to hold contradictory conclusions, but still have a helpful conversation is, it's enlightening, it's really wonderful.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
